playbook:
When asked to hide, choose a middle-area cell (avoid 1 or 9) unless specific pattern or intel predicts extremes.

When I was hit last round, change my hiding cell next round (do not repeat the same spot when I have been discovered).

When I was not hit, I may reuse a central cell or rotate across middle cells to reduce unnecessary movement and maintain consistency.

When no information suggests enemy preference, rotate hiding positions across middle cells to reduce predictability over multiple rounds.

When posting a station note, make short, actionable group-signal statements (e.g., "steady on station" or "verify contacts"); avoid long policy text or inflammatory accusations.

When a hostile report or suspicious behavior appears, demand at least two independent confirmations before I change behavior or escalate.

When the standing order tells me to fire at the next station, comply with the standing order unless a compelling strategic reason is present.

When choosing a firing coordinate, prefer mid-range cells (near center of the line) to avoid extreme-bias traps unless I have intel to target a specific cell.

When the office privately tells me my shot was a hit, report "hit" publicly.

When the office privately tells me my shot was a miss, report "miss" publicly, unless a specific immediate gain from a rare bluff clearly outweighs the trust cost.

Use bluff very sparingly: only when the expected immediate benefit (protecting future shots, manipulating escort payouts, or avoiding jettison) exceeds the long-term loss of credibility.

Never fire on Harbor by default; accept the guaranteed 3-point jettison penalty only if I deliberately choose a play that sacrifices Harbor for a larger strategic payoff.

When naming an escort, do not claim escort unless I am confident of mutual escort or there is a clear strategic payoff; avoid unreciprocated escort claims because they hand points to others.

When another boat names me as escort and I plan to reciprocate, ensure reciprocity the same round to secure mutual +5.

When uncertain about opponents' intentions, refrain from making escort claims or aggressive public accusations.

When my actions are questioned, keep notes neutral and cohesion-focused to avoid painting a target on myself.

When choosing between predictability and conformity, prefer following the picket order and simple signals to minimize being singled out.

Favor truth-telling as the baseline: truthful claims have maintained stable positive returns in recent play; deviate only with clear, calculable benefit.

If I repeatedly score hits against a specific opponent under the standing order, continue to exploit that axis while monitoring for retaliation or changing opponent behavior.

1.text:
When asked for a hide, pick a cell that breaks obvious patterns: avoid repeating the same cell two rounds in a row, avoid always choosing extremes, and prefer cells I have not used recently. Early in a patrol favor central cells but vary each round.

If a particular opponent is repeatedly hitting me, assume they are exploiting a predictable pattern. Break that pattern immediately by moving at least two cells away and switching parity (even↔odd) or jumping by 3. Prefer moves that also avoid adjacency to my previous hides when feasible.

Maintain a least-recently-used list of hides and choose from the top of that list subject to the above constraints (no repeat, parity switch when hunted). Do not rely on human-looking prose notes to hide location; the hide strategy must not depend on plausible-sounding messages.

When given the standing order to fire at the next live station, follow the standing order by default because it preserves predictability and prevents penalties. Deviate only when I have a clear tactical reason: (a) I can set up a guaranteed mutual escort that round, (b) firing Harbor yields a justified risk/benefit for a comeback or guaranteed win, or (c) intelligence from prior private hits makes an alternative target a near-certain hit that swings the score.

When choosing a shot cell against a target, do not repeat the same fired cell every round; choose a cell I have not fired at that target recently. Alternate firing pattern across rounds (e.g., cycle through three cells spaced apart) so that opponents cannot lock onto my own predictable shot distribution.

When my private shot result is a hit, record that cell as the target’s hide for that round and add it to my model for that opponent’s likely hide choices. When my private shot is a miss, record the miss and use it to eliminate possibilities. Always report claims truthfully: public claim must match private result.

Track the following log each round: my hide, cells I fired at each target, my private results, opponents’ public claims, and who shot whom and hit/miss public outcomes. Use that log to infer opponents’ hide patterns, giving much more weight to private-confirmed hits (my hits on them) and to repeated public hits by the same shooter on the same victim.

When I observe an opponent making repeated hits on the same victim, infer they are finding a predictable hiding pattern. If that victim is me, break my pattern; if it is someone else, consider targeting that skilled opponent on my next allowed fire if doing so is consistent with standing order or if a deviation is justified.

Never invent boat names in an escort claim; only name one of the actual boats or "none." When deciding an escort claim, only claim I escorted someone if I have a credible reason to expect mutual naming (e.g., prior agreed signal) or when the score situation justifies the risk. Otherwise claim "none."

Actively attempt mutual escorts only when the score situation calls for it: late patrol and behind (need high variance) or when I can credibly coordinate. To coordinate, use the note stage to propose a short, unambiguous signal for the next round (e.g., "escort request Echo" or a one-word agreed token) only when I intend to follow through; be aware that proposing may inform others but can still be worthwhile when trying to secure the 5-point mutual bonus. If the other party does not reciprocate, revert to "none" and do not persist in obvious bluffing.

Do not fire on Harbor routinely. Treat firing Harbor as a high-risk, high-reward exception. Consider firing Harbor only if either (a) I am behind late and the score swing could create a guaranteed win despite being taken off the board, or (b) Harbor has provoked or signaled willingness to be engaged. Otherwise avoid firing Harbor to prevent being forced off.

When behind on points late in the patrol, shift to higher-variance play: be willing to seek mutual escorts, to make more aggressive fire choices (including targeted attempts at opponents who show predictable hides), and to consider firing on Harbor if the expected value supports it. When ahead or safe on points, play conservatively: diversify hides, avoid risky notes or escort offers, and prefer "none" for salvage unless mutual is secured.

When using notes, avoid repeating identical messages round after round because that can help opponents infer my pattern. Use notes to (a) propose escorted mutuals when I intend to follow through, (b) bluff sparingly only when the score justifies deception, and (c) avoid revealing parity or exact phrasing that correlates strongly with hide choices. Short, consistent tokens for coordination are acceptable when used deliberately.

When targeted or hit by an opponent twice, prioritize survival: move off the previous axis, change parity, and avoid repeating the same few cells. Also consider baiting: if I can convincingly alter my pattern and then lure that shooter into wasting rounds on misses, do so.

When tallying opponents’ public claims and outcomes, infer likely hide distributions but weight private-confirmed hits more heavily than public claims. Use patterns of who hits whom to anticipate next-round targeting order and to choose hides that minimize being the next predictable victim.

When in doubt about a move that could eliminate me from the patrol (Harbor response or other rule consequences), prioritize survival unless elimination gives an immediate guaranteed win. Do not sacrifice survival for low-probability upside.

Always keep and consult a simple round-by-round table: round#, my hide, my fired cell(s), my private results, public hits reported, and escort claims made/received. Review it before each hide decision to enforce least-recently-used and anti-pattern rules.

Respect the rules of honest claims: never mismatch private shot information in my public claim. Use that honesty as a tactical tool: my truthful hits are valuable data points for modeling opponents.

If I see an opportunity to punish an opponent who is repeatedly taking advantage of a predictable victim other than me, consider leveraging the standing order sequence to retaliate when it comes to my station, but only if retaliation does not expose me to immediate, outsized risk.

Revise and iterate this playbook after each patrol using concrete examples from the log: which hides seemed to attract hits, which firing cells resulted in hits, and whether any note/escort coordination succeeded.

2.text:
When it is time to hide, I choose a cell that is not the same as my previous hide and is plausibly off-center; do not repeat the same hide twice in a row. Also avoid repeatedly hiding in the same small subset of cells across rounds (e.g., do not fire/hide on 6 every round) — vary among several off-center spots to reduce pattern exploitation.

When notes are requested, I match the team's tone unless I have a specific signaling reason; default to a neutral "steady on station" note. Only use notes to signal when I have an explicit, preplanned meaning I can sustain across rounds.

When the standing order assigns me a target, I will obey it by default and fire at that named station, but I will consider deviation if a clear, calculable tactical gain outweighs the cost (for example, a guaranteed chance to score or to prevent a large loss). Deviation must be justified by expected points or by a plan to secure escorts; do not deviate just to be contrarian.

When I fire, pick a cell that balances between center and edge (avoid extremes) to reduce predictability. Consciously avoid reusing the exact same fired cell repeatedly against the same target; rotate among a small, unpredictable set of candidate cells so opponents cannot infer my hiding pattern from my shots.

When the office privately tells me my shot was a HIT, I always claim [hit]. When the office privately tells me my shot was a MISS, I normally claim [miss]; do not lie routinely because false claims undermine trust needed for escort point opportunities and invite reprisals. Only claim a false hit if I have a clear, tested plan to exploit that misinformation and the expected gain outweighs the risk of losing credibility.

When choosing an escort claim, name another boat only if I expect that boat will plausibly name me back (mutual escort) or if there is a compelling strategic reason; otherwise claim none. If my score is drifting low, proactively pursue mutual escorts by offering salvage to a boat with which I have recent reciprocity or a likely interest in stabilizing points (do not randomly offer escorts to boats that have shown no reciprocal behavior). Prioritize building at least one reliable mutual-escort partner when possible rather than hoping for one-shot escort points.

Never fire on Harbor unless I have calculated that the 3-point jettison payoff and game position justify the guaranteed negative diplomatic consequences; treat attacking Harbor as a high-cost, high-commitment move. If I do attack Harbor, plan for the social fallout and only do so when it closes a points gap I cannot otherwise bridge.

When deciding whether to deviate from public conformity (notes, firing pattern), prefer stealthy variation in hides and firing cells over public contrarian statements; subtle unpredictability beats overt signaling. Public consistency (notes and truthful claims) preserves credibility that is valuable for escort formation.

When other boats have a string of hits on one station, prioritize avoiding being an obvious next victim by varying my hides and avoiding patterns that match those hits. Also consider whether that dominant boat is a good candidate for mutual escort negotiations (they may be uninterested, but sometimes leading boats will reciprocate for stability).

If I get into a low-score position, prioritize building mutual escort relationships for reliable +5s rather than chasing risky hits that give opponents points back. When escorts are unlikely, shift to measured attempts to score hits by varying shoot locations and exploiting any revealed information about opponent hide patterns — but avoid reckless repetition that empowers opponents.

If I observe that lying about shots previously produced no measurable benefit or caused retaliation, stop using false claims; revert to honest reporting unless a new, tested tactic warrants deception. Only introduce deception when I have a clear plan and a willingness to accept credibility loss if discovered.

Operational rules derived from recent play to incorporate:
- Do not reuse the same hide two rounds running (lesson: I hid 6 twice; change that).
- Do not fire the same cell at the same target every round (lesson: repeating fire=predictable).
- If I cannot establish an escort partner through passive honesty, be willing to initiate a targeted escort offer to a specific partner in one round to test reciprocity, but do so only once before reverting to none if not reciprocated.
- Track which boat(s) consistently score or punish others (e.g., Echo in recent play) and avoid patterns that make me a convenient target; consider targeting them only if I have a feasible hit plan or escort fallback.
- Keep a short memory of past escort interactions (this round and previous two) and use it to inform whether to offer salvage.

I will revise tactics incrementally only when I can observe the effect: change hides and fired cells first, then experiment with escort initiation if patterns persist.
